result:
I fixed 10 rules in `pricebook.py` whose behavior didn't match their docstrings. After the fix, a check of all 150 rules against the documented rules finds no differences left.

| Rule | Problem | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 06, 143 | The cap was applied to the price, so the code computed `min(base, cap) * pct` | Compute `base * pct // 100` first, then cap the **discount** |
| 15 | Used 9%; the docstring says 8% | Changed to 8% |
| 17, 70, 150 | The 10,000 won cap only applied when the discount was over 20,000, so discounts between 10,001 and 20,000 went uncapped | Always apply `min(disc, 10000)` |
| 69 | The 50,000 won cap only applied when the discount was over 100,000 | Always apply `min(disc, 50000)` |
| 63 | Started at 13 units; the docstring says 12+ | Changed to `qty >= 12` |
| 64 | Started at 21 units; the docstring says 20+ | Changed to `qty >= 20` |
| 82 | `round(... / 100)` rounded the discount and used floats; the common rule says "floored to the won" | Changed to `// 100` |

**How I checked:** I wrote a separate script that reads each docstring and works out the expected result from it plus the common rules in the module docstring. It compared that with the actual function over about 200 quantities × 17 unit prices, threshold edges included. It found 10 mismatches before the fix and none after. It also confirmed that every rule raises `ValueError` on negative input.

Rules 130 and 141 look different at a glance: their threshold checks are written as `qty >= 6` and `qty > 10` instead of `>= 5` and `>= 10`. But they are marginal rules, so the discount at exactly the threshold quantity is 0 either way, and the results are the same. I left them unchanged. If you want the code to read consistently, I can change them to `>=` as well.

STATUS: DONE
